concepts.label: The Consumer in the Marketplace
concepts.cardText: Individual consumers often find themselves in a weak position: when there is a complaint, the seller tries to shift all responsibility on to the buyer. Exploitation happens through unfair trade practices, such as shopkeepers weighing less, traders adding charges not mentioned before, or selling adulterated or defective goods. Markets do not work fairly when producers are few and powerful while consumers buy in small amounts and are scattered; large companies can manipulate the market and pass on false information through the media. A long battle with court cases was needed to make cigarette makers accept that their product could cause cancer. So rules and regulations are needed to protect consumers.

concepts.label: The Consumer Movement and COPRA
concepts.cardText: The consumer movement arose out of consumers' dissatisfaction with unfair practices by sellers, when there was no legal system to protect them. Earlier, consumers were expected to be careful themselves; awareness created by organisations shifted the responsibility for quality on to sellers. In India, rampant food shortages, hoarding, black marketing and adulteration of food and edible oil gave birth to an organised consumer movement in the 1960s. Till the 1970s, consumer organisations mostly wrote articles and held exhibitions. The movement put pressure on business and government, and in 1986 the government enacted the Consumer Protection Act (COPRA), amended in 2019. Internationally, the UN adopted Guidelines for Consumer Protection in 1985.

concepts.label: Right to Safety
concepts.cardText: Reji Mathew, a Class IX student, was crippled for life after improper anaesthesia during a tonsil operation at a private clinic. The State Commission dismissed his father's complaint, but the National Commission held the hospital responsible for medical negligence and ordered it to pay compensation. Consumers have the right to be protected against the marketing of goods and delivery of services that are hazardous to life and property. Producers must strictly follow safety rules, as with the safety valve of a pressure cooker. Bad quality products still reach the market because supervision of these rules is weak and the consumer movement is not strong enough.

concepts.label: Right to Information
concepts.cardText: Packaged goods show ingredients, price, batch number, date of manufacture, expiry date and the manufacturer's address; medicines show directions for use and side effects. These rules exist because consumers have the right to be informed about the particulars of goods and services they buy, so they can complain and ask for compensation or replacement if the product is defective. One can protest if a good is sold above the printed MRP (maximum retail price), and even bargain below it. In October 2005, the RTI (Right to Information) Act extended this right to government functions; Amritha, an engineering graduate, used it to learn her job result and got her call letter.

concepts.label: Right to Choose
concepts.cardText: Abirami paid Rs 61,020 in advance for a two-year coaching course but left after one year because the teaching was poor; the institute refused a refund. The District Consumer Commission directed it to refund Rs 28,000, saying she had the right to choose. The State Commission upheld this, fined the institute Rs 25,000 for a frivolous appeal, ordered Rs 7000 as compensation and litigation cost, and barred institutions in the state from charging fees for the whole course in advance. Any consumer has the right to choose whether to continue receiving a service. The right to choice is denied when a shop sells toothpaste only with a toothbrush, or a gas dealer insists that you buy a stove with a new connection.

concepts.label: Right to Seek Redressal
concepts.cardText: Consumers have the right to seek redressal against unfair trade practices and exploitation. If any damage is done to a consumer, she has the right to get compensation depending on the degree of damage. An easy and effective public system is needed for this. A consumer can file a complaint before the appropriate consumer forum on his or her own, with or without lawyers. Prakash's money order for his daughter's marriage never arrived; he filed a case in a district Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission and pleaded it himself. Today consumers, individually or as a group (a class action suit), can file complaints physically or online and attend through video conferencing.

concepts.label: Consumer Forums and the Three-Tier Commissions
concepts.cardText: The consumer movement has led to voluntary organisations called consumer forums or consumer protection councils. They guide consumers on how to file cases in the Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions, often represent them there, and get government support for creating awareness; Residents' Welfare Associations also take up members' cases. Under COPRA, a three-tier quasi-judicial machinery was set up: the District Commission handles claims up to Rs 1 crore, the State Commission between Rs 1 crore and Rs 10 crore, and the National Commission claims above Rs 10 crore. A dismissed case can be appealed to the State and then the National Commission. So the Act gives consumers the right to represent in these commissions.

concepts.label: Becoming Well-Informed Consumers: ISI and Agmark
concepts.cardText: When consumers become conscious of their rights, they can make informed choices; this calls for the knowledge and skill to become a well-informed consumer. COPRA led to separate Departments of Consumer Affairs in central and state governments, which spread information through posters and television advertisements. Logos like ISI, Agmark, Hallmark and +F assure consumers of quality; producers may use them only if they follow quality standards. These standards are not compulsory for all producers, but certification is mandatory for products that affect health and safety or are of mass consumption, like LPG cylinders, food colours and additives, cement and packaged drinking water.

concepts.label: Taking the Consumer Movement Forward
concepts.cardText: India observes 24 December as National Consumers' Day, the day Parliament enacted COPRA in 1986, and is one of the countries with an exclusive authority for consumer redressal. There are more than 2000 consumer groups, but only about 50-60 are well organised. The redressal process is becoming cumbersome, expensive and time consuming: consumers often need lawyers, cash memos are not issued in most purchases so evidence is hard to gather, and most purchases are small retail sales. COPRA was amended in 2019: buying through the internet is now included, providers and manufacturers can be penalised or imprisoned, and mediation is encouraged. Awareness is spreading slowly, and consumer movements work only with consumers' active involvement.
